toc.title: Feel it instead of reacting to it
What safety looks like in a boundary
Seeing the future from safety, not defense

blocks.p: What does the ventral vagal safety state have to do with setting boundaries? It seems like there's a balance there: safety, but also sympathetic flight and fight. That question is dead on, so let's walk through it.
When we enforce a boundary, there is some flight or fight activation. I would lean more toward the fight activation.

Not angry, not lashing out, not name calling. I suppose that's a boundary too, but it comes with less ventral vagal activation. Ideally, we want as much grounding and as much anchoring in safety as we can.

I think it's totally okay for boundaries to come across as strong. A very clear no. A very strong no. Maybe even a raised-voice no, if needed. Some people, in some situations, might need that. But you can do that from a strong anchoring in your ventral vagal safety state.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Feel it instead of reacting to it

blocks.p: So what needs to happen? In the moment, we feel that activation. There's a spike, a surge of wanting to get out of here. Then it changes into irritation: this person isn't picking up on my cues, and they're trampling all over my boundary, or my values, or whatever it is.

Once we get more into that fight activation, that's where we'd put in something like, "I'm not okay with that." Flight activation could look like, "I hear you. I don't need to be a part of this. I'm going to leave now."

But that requires that we feel and embrace the activation, rather than feeling it unconsciously and then reacting to it. We need a net, metaphorically, to capture that activation inward. It's hard in the moment, but in the moment we'd say to ourselves something like: "It's there. I have every right to feel this way. And I can come from compassion." That compassion can come from assuming this person maybe doesn't know any better.

All of that takes a strong anchoring in safety. Ideally, when we're in these situations, we'd already be familiar with what the defensive activation feels like, so that when it shows up, it's not overwhelming. And we'd already have a good amount of safety in our system, because we've practiced feeling safety. With the right balance, those two things add up to noticing the activation, acting on it, enforcing a boundary, and following through with it.

I don't think there's a single answer for setting a boundary in the moment, when you're feeling it and you didn't expect it. That's the hardest. It always comes down to proactively practicing these things ahead of time. That means proactively practicing safety, but also proactively feeling into defense and mentally rehearsing it.
Say you know you typically feel freeze in social situations, especially challenging ones. Here are three ways to practice, from most approachable to most challenging:

ol: Feel into what's already there. When you're not in that situation, practice safety, and then feel into the freeze activation you know is going to happen anyway. That's a generally approachable way, as long as you have enough safety.

Remember it. "I feel this often. I've felt it in the past, and I'm going to feel it again in the future." Anchor into safety, then remember what it feels like to be in that situation. Maybe even remember a specific incident. Let it be there, and then pendulate it with safety.
Imagine it. This one is very challenging. "I know I'm going to feel this anyway." Imagine a scenario where you feel it, and then do the pendulation.

blocks.p: All of these act as buffers, inoculations against a real-life scenario in the future.

blocks.h: What safety looks like in a boundary

blocks.p: So in a relationship where a boundary is needed, the safety state is what lets you stay connected and still enforce the boundary. What does the ventral piece look like?

Internally, it could show up as deep compassion for the person. You smile and you say, "Look, you sound ridiculous. I love you, but no, I can't go there with you." That would be a really soft way to approach it, with lots of compassion. It's not easy to do.

Or it could be a little firmer: "Look, this is inappropriate. I care about you. I know you have the best intentions, but I think you're way off base, and I can't go down this path with you." That's firmer, but it still comes from enough ventral activation to remember: I do care about this person.

The more interesting piece, I think, is the connection with yourself, and I think that takes a lot of ventral activation too. The safety state is connection with others, with self, and with the environment. So part of the puzzle is: I'm connected to myself. I know what I feel. I feel that activation. It makes sense, it's there for a reason, and I can let it be there. I'm also connected to what I believe, what I know, what I like. And I'm connected to my values, like the value that I can't compromise certain things. Morally, I just can't do that.

All of that is a very strong foundation. I think it comes from ventral, but probably also from some fight activation, because there's empowerment there. Behaviorally, that might come across compassionately and softly, or a little more toward the firm no. But once we're lashing out and name calling, that behavior probably suggests there's less ventral activation.

blocks.h: Seeing the future from safety, not defense

blocks.p: When we're in sympathetic activation, we tell the story through that lens, and we expect the other person to come back at us. We know what's going to happen. They're going to say this. They're a jerk. That's the tricky part of the distorted lens.

But when we have enough ventral activation, we can still "see the future," in quotes. "I know this person, and realistically, they're going to lash out. We've spent enough time together that I know. Dammit, I can't do this anymore. I'm going to embrace the fact that they're going to do this, and I'm going to hold my ground. And if they cross a certain boundary, I'm going to leave." That's telling the future in a sense, but it's very much grounded in reality. Flight, fight, freeze, and shutdown tell the future too, but that's more fear driven, more driven by defense and dysregulation. In the moment, that's really hard to parse out, and maybe unrealistic. So ahead of time might be the best time to know what's realistically going to happen.

That knowing is a big piece. Actual knowing, not dysregulated assuming. I know this person, I know their behavior, and I know how they're likely to react. And here I am, firmly aware of how I feel, what I know to be true, and what I will or will not do morally. And I don't control them. That's actually a big part of it: knowing I don't control them, but realistically knowing how they're going to react. I have no choice but to live up to what I know is right or wrong, or the line I will or will not cross. I'm firmly planted, like a tree deeply rooted in the ground.
That's different than stubbornness. I'm not talking about stubbornness. I'm talking about values, principles, morality. I just can't do this thing they're asking me to do, however it shows up.

Being solidly rooted in yourself also means letting the chips fall where they may. I don't control them. They're likely going to do whatever it is they're going to do. If they act on it, the results could be disastrous for them or for the people around them. And there might be some level of: whatever happens, happens. I can't control it. I'll do the best I can. Depending on the situation, I'll look out for those I love, and I'll look out for myself. But this outcome is out of my control. If they're going to make disastrous decisions, I just can't control that.

No, it's not easy. Some relationships are easier to hold a boundary in than others. Ultimately, I think it comes down to a strong enough connection with yourself, and the ability to feel your sympathetic states and turn them into empowerment.

It also means understanding that the other person is going to make their own choices, and they need to live with the consequences of those choices. You don't control the outcome of their choices, and maybe you shouldn't try to impose your control on it.
